div.head: Chapter 2
div.p: There are four categories of unbelievers, and accordingly we must deal with them in four different ways. Ignorance of this principle has been chiefly responsible for all the destruction of the Indies, as will become clear from what is said below.

This principle is proved by running through each category in turn. The first is that there are some unbelievers who dwell among Christians and are subject to Christian princes or kings, such as the Jews and the Moors who used to live in Castile, whom we called Mudéjar Moors. Concerning these unbelievers, many ecclesiastical and secular laws and decrees have been written and established, as appears throughout the title on Jews and Saracens in the Decretals, and in the decrees and in the human laws, ut Codex, de Judeis, et Codex, de paganis, etc.

These unbelievers who live as unbelievers, insofar as they live under the lordship and jurisdiction or principality of Christian kings, are subjects of those kings both in law and in fact, and are therefore bound to observe the just laws imposed on them, living according to them as every subject must observe those of the prince or superior under whose jurisdiction and district he lives, as is self-evident; and both canon and civil law are full of this.

There are four kinds of subjects according to the laws. The first, by reason of domicile, residence, or habitation. The second, by reason of one's own origin or birth, or that of one's parents. The third, by reason of offenses, if someone commits a wrong in another's land or jurisdiction or enters into some contract there. The fourth, by reason of suit, homage, and vassalage, as in the case of those who hold some fief, etc.

The second category or kind of unbelievers is and are those who hold the lands, dominions, and things they possess in fact but against all right; that is to say: those who have usurped them by violence, unjustly, from the Christian people, such as the Moors and Turks, through wars or through any other unjust or tyrannical means, as is evident in the case of those who detain the Holy Land and Africa and all of Asia and part of Hungary, and many other parts and kingdoms that once belonged to Christendom. Of this second kind are those who are not content with holding our lands and kingdoms under usurpation, but with all their forces assail the Christian commonwealth with their cruel and arrogant armies and wars, killing and capturing the members of Christ, as we see and grieve over each day, whose chief aim is, if they could, to impede, destroy, and annihilate the faith and name of Christ, and to spread their abominable sect. And these are properly enemies of the faith and of the Christian religion.

These, by reason of the offenses, most grievous injuries and wrongs that they commit against the Christian people, are subjects of the Church in law but not in fact, on account of their great and brutish forces and power; and consequently, whenever the Church is able, or its members who are the Christian princes are able, they may punish and chastise them as delinquent subjects. Of these treats Saint Thomas, 2.2, q. 10, a. 8, where he says that against these the Church has four legal avenues for proceeding against them. The first, by right of recovery, to reclaim the kingdoms and lands that they have unjustly usurped from us, as is proved in 23, q. 2, c. dominus noster et q. 4, c. fortitudo, et [q. 8] c. dispar et c. igitur, et c. omni timore, et c. hortatu et c. olim causa. De restitutione spoliatorum.
The second, by right of defense, and this is clear, because even a private person is permitted to defend themselves, L. ut vim, ff. Digest. De iustitia et iure.

The third, by right of vengeance, punishment, or retribution, because any prince who recognizes no superior may not only wage war to defend himself and recover what has been usurped from him, but also punish and chastise those who have done him wrong, 23, q. 1, c. quid culpatur.

The fourth, by right of liberation, to free oppressed Christians whom they hold captive with tyrannical fury, q. 3, c. Maximianus, et per totam illam quaestionem et c. 8, c. scire vos oportet; et q. 5, c. regum officium. And more will be said on this below.
